claim: Artificial stimulation of Agouti-Related Peptide (AgRP) neurons promotes intense food consumption.
source: Artificial stimulation of Agouti-Related Peptide (AgRP) neurons promotes intense food consumption, yet paradoxically during natural behavior these cells are inhibited before feeding begins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding in the field.

claim: During natural behavior, AgRP neurons are inhibited before feeding begins.
source: Artificial stimulation of Agouti-Related Peptide (AgRP) neurons promotes intense food consumption, yet paradoxically during natural behavior these cells are inhibited before feeding begins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Brief stimulation of AgRP neurons can generate hunger that persists for tens of minutes.
source: Previously, to reconcile these observations, we showed that brief stimulation of AgRP neurons can generate hunger that persists for tens of minutes, but the mechanisms underlying this sustained hunger drive remain unknown (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Neuropeptide Y (NPY) is uniquely required for the long-lasting effects of AgRP neurons on feeding behavior.
source: Here we show that Neuropeptide Y (NPY) is uniquely required for the long-lasting effects of AgRP neurons on feeding behavior.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of NPY abolished optically-stimulated feeding.
source: Deletion of NPY, but not AgRP or GABA, abolished optically-stimulated feeding, and this was rescued by NPY re-expression selectively in AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of AgRP did not abolish optically-stimulated feeding.
source: Deletion of NPY, but not AgRP or GABA, abolished optically-stimulated feeding, and this was rescued by NPY re-expression selectively in AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1E.

claim: Deletion of GABA did not abolish optically-stimulated feeding.
source: Deletion of NPY, but not AgRP or GABA, abolished optically-stimulated feeding, and this was rescued by NPY re-expression selectively in AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1F.

claim: NPY re-expression selectively in AgRP neurons rescued the feeding phenotype in NPY knockout mice.
source: Deletion of NPY, but not AgRP or GABA, abolished optically-stimulated feeding, and this was rescued by NPY re-expression selectively in AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3L-P.

claim: NPY sustains hunger in the interval between food discovery and consumption.
source: These findings reveal a unique role for NPY in sustaining hunger in the interval between food discovery and consumption.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental findings.

claim: AgRP neurons are a small population of cells in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
source: AgRP neurons are a small population of cells in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus that are critical for regulating food intake (Andermann and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: AgRP neurons are critical for regulating food intake.
source: AgRP neurons are a small population of cells in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus that are critical for regulating food intake (Andermann and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: AgRP neurons are progressively activated during food deprivation.
source: These cells are progressively activated during food deprivation (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Hahn et al., 1998; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015), in part due to fluctuations in nutritionally-regulated hormones such as leptin and ghrelin (Beutler et al., 2017; Blouet and Schwartz, 2010; Cowley et al., 2001; Cowley et al., 2003; Dietrich et al., 2013; Nakazato et al., 2001; Pinto et al., 2004; Schneeberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: AgRP neuron activation during food deprivation is in part due to fluctuations in nutritionally-regulated hormones such as leptin and ghrelin.
source: These cells are progressively activated during food deprivation (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Hahn et al., 1998; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015), in part due to fluctuations in nutritionally-regulated hormones such as leptin and ghrelin (Beutler et al., 2017; Blouet and Schwartz, 2010; Cowley et al., 2001; Cowley et al., 2003; Dietrich et al., 2013; Nakazato et al., 2001; Pinto et al., 2004; Schneeberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food seeking and consumption.
source: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food seeking and consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011), whereas silencing of these cells leads to aphagia or starvation (Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Silencing of AgRP neurons leads to aphagia or starvation.
source: Optogenetic or chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons promotes intense food seeking and consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011), whereas silencing of these cells leads to aphagia or starvation (Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: AgRP neurons play a key role in the homeostatic negative feedback loop that links the need for energy to the stimulation of feeding behavior.
source: Thus AgRP neurons play a key role in the homeostatic negative feedback loop that links the need for energy to the stimulation of feeding behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the cited literature.

claim: AgRP neurons are inhibited within seconds when a hungry animal sees or smells food.
source: Although AgRP neurons are gradually activated during fasting, they are inhibited within seconds when a hungry animal sees or smells food (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons often occurs before a single bite of food has been consumed.
source: Paradoxically, this rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons often occurs before a single bite of food has been consumed and then persists for the duration of the ensuing meal.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on cited observations.

claim: The rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons persists for the duration of the ensuing meal.
source: Paradoxically, this rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons often occurs before a single bite of food has been consumed and then persists for the duration of the ensuing meal.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on cited observations.

claim: Brief optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons in the absence of food can drive voracious food intake tens of minutes later, long after AgRP neuron stimulation has been terminated.
source: Consistent with this, we showed that brief optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons in the absence of food can drive voracious food intake tens of minutes later, long after AgRP neuron stimulation has been terminated (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: AgRP neurons can generate an unusual 'sustained hunger drive' that outlasts their acute firing.
source: This indicates that AgRP neurons can generate an unusual 'sustained hunger drive' that outlasts their acute firing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AgRP neurons release three neurotransmitters that can influence feeding: AgRP, NPY and GABA.
source: AgRP neurons release three neurotransmitters that can influence feeding: AgRP, NPY and GABA (Andermann and Lowell, 2017; Hahn et al., 1998; Krashes et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons for 15 minutes produced robust food intake in mice lacking GABA or AgRP signaling.
source: This pre-stimulation paradigm produced robust food intake in mice lacking GABA or AgRP signaling, and the magnitude of food consumption was similar between mutants and littermate controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pre-stimulation of mice lacking NPY caused no increase in food intake.
source: In striking contrast, pre-stimulation of mice lacking NPY caused no increase in food intake (Figure 1C, bottom row).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Control mice, as well as mice lacking GABA or AgRP, showed a clear dose-response relationship between pre-stimulation duration and total food intake.
source: We found that control mice, as well as mice lacking GABA or AgRP, showed a clear dose-response relationship between pre-stimulation duration and total food intake (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 1E, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in food intake following AgRP neuron pre-stimulation was due to an increase in bout size, rather than bout number.
source: This increase in food intake was due to an increase in bout size, rather than bout number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NPY- mice showed no dose-dependent increase in food intake following longer durations of AgRP neuron pre-stimulation.
source: In contrast NPY- mice showed no dose-dependent increase in food intake following longer durations of AgRP neuron pre-stimulation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The behavioral defect in NPY- mice was not due to a failure to activate AgRP neurons.
source: This behavioral defect was not due to a failure to activate AgRP neurons, because we observed robust Fos expression in AgRP neurons after optogenetic stimulation of NPY- mice (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1L.

claim: NPY is specifically required for the sustained hunger produced by AgRP neuron activation.
source: Instead this indicates that NPY is specifically required for the sustained hunger produced by AgRP neuron activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: All genotypes except for NPY- mice exhibited robust food consumption that gradually declined with increasing delay duration up to 60 min.
source: We found that all genotypes except for NPY- mice exhibited robust food consumption that gradually declined with increasing delay duration up to 60 min (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 1I-K.

claim: The hunger signal generated by AgRP neurons has a rise time of approximately four minutes.
source: By pooling data from all control animals, we estimated that this hunger signal has a rise time of approximately four minutes (logarithmic growth; N = 23; R-Square = 0.72; Figure 1M) and a decay-time of approximately 47 min (exponential decay; N = 19; R-Square = 0.87; Figure 1N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1M.

claim: The hunger signal generated by AgRP neurons has a decay-time of approximately 47 min.
source: By pooling data from all control animals, we estimated that this hunger signal has a rise time of approximately four minutes (logarithmic growth; N = 23; R-Square = 0.72; Figure 1M) and a decay-time of approximately 47 min (exponential decay; N = 19; R-Square = 0.87; Figure 1N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1N.

claim: AgRP neuron activity rapidly generates a durable, NPY-dependent signal that drives feeding behavior.
source: This indicates that AgRP neuron activity rapidly generates a durable, NPY-dependent signal that drives feeding behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Vigorous lever pressing was observed following pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons in AgRP- and GABA- mice, as well as controls.
source: We observed vigorous lever pressing following pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons in AgRP- and GABA- mice, as well as controls (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 2B-F.

claim: Pre-stimulation had no effect on operant responding in animals lacking NPY.
source: In contrast pre-stimulation had no effect on operant responding in animals lacking NPY (Figure 2B,C,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2F.

claim: NPY is critical for the ability of AgRP neurons to drive food seeking behavior as well as food consumption.
source: This indicates that NPY is critical for the ability of AgRP neurons to drive food seeking behavior as well as food consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the operant behavior experiments.

claim: In control mice, alternating stimulation protocol stimulated robust food consumption.
source: In control mice, this protocol stimulated robust food consumption (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Food intake was equally distributed between the Laser ON and OFF epochs in control mice.
source: Importantly, food intake was equally distributed between the Laser ON and OFF epochs (Figure 3C–I), indicating that wild-type animals do not distinguish the boundary between these two-minute intervals, presumbly due to the sustained hunger produced by AgRP neuron stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3C-I.

claim: Loss of NPY caused food intake to become strictly time-locked to the laser stimulus.
source: Remarkably, loss of NPY caused food intake to become strictly time-locked to the laser stimulus: that is, NPY- animals ate during concurrent stimulation, but then stopped eating within seconds of the laser shutting off (Figure 3C,D,F,I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3C, 3D, 3F, and 3I.

claim: Mice lacking GABA or AgRP signaling, as well as their littermate controls, showed no difference in feeding between the Laser ON and OFF periods.
source: In contrast, mice lacking GABA or AgRP signaling, as well as their littermate controls, showed no difference in feeding between the Laser ON and OFF periods (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3E-H.

claim: In the absence of NPY, AgRP neuron driven hunger dissipates within seconds of the offset of AgRP neuron firing.
source: This indicates that, in the absence of NPY, AgRP neuron driven hunger dissipates within seconds of the offset of AgRP neuron firing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the alternating stimulation experiments.

claim: NPY is expressed in cell types other than AgRP neurons.
source: NPY is expressed in cell types other than AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as background knowledge.

claim: Mice injected with AAV expressing NPY, but not GFP, showed restoration of NPY expression in the ARC.
source: Mice injected with AAV expressing NPY, but not GFP, showed restoration of NPY expression in the ARC (Figure 3K) and complete rescue of the feeding phenotypes associated with NPY- knockout (Figure 3L–P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3K-P.

claim: NPY re-expression in AgRP neurons caused complete rescue of the feeding phenotypes associated with NPY- knockout.
source: Mice injected with AAV expressing NPY, but not GFP, showed restoration of NPY expression in the ARC (Figure 3K) and complete rescue of the feeding phenotypes associated with NPY- knockout (Figure 3L–P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3L-P.

claim: NPY re-expression in AgRP neurons caused feeding behavior in NPY- mice to become uncoupled from the onset and offset of laser stimulation, in a way that was indistinguishable from wild-type animals.
source: For example, NPY re-expression in AgRP neurons caused feeding behavior in NPY- mice to become uncoupled from the onset and offset of laser stimulation, in a way that was indistinguishable from wild-type animals (Figure 3N–P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 3N-P.

claim: The phenotypes observed in NPY- mice are due to loss of NPY expression in AgRP neurons, rather than effects of this mutation on other circuits or development.
source: This indicates that the phenotypes observed in NPY- mice are due to loss of NPY expression in AgRP neurons, rather than effects of this mutation on other circuits or development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the rescue experiments.

claim: Concurrent chemogenetic stimulation increased food consumption in mice lacking NPY.
source: We found that concurrent chemogenetic stimulation increased food consumption in mice lacking NPY (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with a previous report (Krashes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 4C, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During concurrent optogenetic stimulation NPY- mice consumed only a small fraction of the food consumed by NPY+ controls.
source: In contrast, during concurrent optogenetic stimulation NPY- mice consumed only a small fraction of the food consumed by NPY+ controls (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Food intake in NPY- mice could be partially rescued by using a higher intensity optogenetic stimulation protocol.
source: We could partially rescue food intake in NPY- mice by using a higher intensity optogenetic stimulation protocol (Figure 4F), whereas NPY+ controls showed no difference in food consumption between high and moderate intensity stimulation (high intensity refers to continuous 20 Hz stimulation, whereas moderate intensity refers to 20 Hz stimulation in a 2 s ON, 3 s OFF pattern; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Intense concurrent optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons can partially overcome the requirement for NPY, likely through increased release of GABA.
source: This indicates that intense concurrent optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons can partially overcome the requirement for NPY, likely through increased release of GABA (Atasoy et al., 2012; Krashes et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the data with citations.

claim: Increased stimulation intensity could not compensate to any degree for loss of NPY in a pre-stimulation paradigm.
source: In contrast to these variable responses to concurrent stimulation, we found that increased stimulation intensity could not compensate to any degree for loss of NPY in a pre-stimulation paradigm (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Endogenous GABA and AgRP are unable to drive food intake effectively on the timescale of sustained hunger (tens of minutes immediately after the offset of stimulation).
source: This is presumably because endogenous GABA and AgRP are unable to drive food intake effectively on the timescale of sustained hunger (tens of minutes immediately after the offset of stimulation).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Infusion of picomoles of NPY into the PVH can elicit voracious food intake.
source: Early studies showed that infusion of picomoles of NPY into the PVH can elicit voracious food intake (Clark et al., 1985; Stanley and Leibowitz, 1984), identifying NPY as an unusually potent orexigen.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: NPY is highly expressed in hunger-promoting AgRP neurons.
source: Consistent with this, NPY is highly expressed in hunger-promoting AgRP neurons (Hahn et al., 1998), and its expression in these cells is increased by energy deficit (Sahu et al., 1988; White and Kershaw, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: NPY expression in AgRP neurons is increased by energy deficit.
source: Consistent with this, NPY is highly expressed in hunger-promoting AgRP neurons (Hahn et al., 1998), and its expression in these cells is increased by energy deficit (Sahu et al., 1988; White and Kershaw, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Genetic deletion of NPY, alone or in combination with AgRP, had little effect on food intake or body weight.
source: However genetic deletion of NPY, alone (Erickson et al., 1996) or in combination with AgRP (Qian et al., 2002), had little effect on food intake or body weight.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Deletion of NPY receptors, alone or in combination, failed to produce the expected lean phenotype.
source: Similarly deletion of NPY receptors, alone (Kushi et al., 1998; Marsh et al., 1998; Pedrazzini et al., 1998) or in combination (Nguyen et al., 2012), failed to produce the expected lean phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Food intake following chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons requires either NPY or GABA signaling, but not both.
source: One study found that food intake following chemogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons requires either NPY or GABA signaling, but not both (Krashes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Antagonists of NPY or GABA receptors in PVH could partially block feeding induced by optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons.
source: Another study showed that antagonists of NPY or GABA receptors in PVH could partially block feeding induced by optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons (Atasoy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: NPY and GABA have partially redundant functions in mediating food intake by AgRP neurons.
source: Taken together, these observations have led to a general view that NPY and GABA have partially redundant functions in mediating food intake by AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the prevailing view in the field.

claim: NPY plays a remarkably specific role in extending the duration of AgRP neurons' behavioral effects for tens of minutes beyond the window of their immediate firing.
source: This revealed a remarkably specific role for NPY in extending the duration of AgRP neurons' behavioral effects for tens of minutes beyond the window of their immediate firing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: NPY provides a molecular correlate for the long-lasting hunger signal that bridges AgRP neuron dynamics with feeding behavior.
source: This in turn provides a molecular correlate for the long-lasting hunger signal that bridges AgRP neuron dynamics with feeding behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: Infusion of AgRP into the brain or stimulation of AgRP release can cause modulation of feeding behavior that persists for days.
source: For example, infusion of AgRP into the brain (Hagan et al., 2000) or stimulation of AgRP release (Krashes et al., 2013; Nakajima et al., 2016) can cause modulation of feeding behavior that persists for days.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Long-lasting potentiation of feeding behavior by AgRP requires several hours to emerge when endogenous AgRP release is stimulated.
source: However, this long-lasting potentiation of feeding behavior requires several hours to emerge when endogenous AgRP release is stimulated (Krashes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: The AgRP peptide is not required for the intense food consumption that occurs immediately following AgRP neuron pre-stimulation.
source: Consistent with this, we find no evidence that the AgRP peptide is required for the intense food consumption that occurs immediately following AgRP neuron pre-stimulation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: NPY and AgRP play complementary roles in the regulation of feeding, with NPY sustaining hunger selectively on the timescale of a meal (tens of minutes after food discovery), whereas AgRP modulates the tone of the feeding circuit over longer timescales.
source: Thus our data suggest that NPY and AgRP play complementary roles in the regulation of feeding, with NPY sustaining hunger selectively on the timescale of a meal (tens of minutes after food discovery), whereas AgRP modulates the tone of the feeding circuit over longer timescales.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: Slice recordings have shown that NPY can have persistent effects on membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release in vitro.
source: Slice recordings have shown that NPY can have persistent effects on membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release in vitro (Dubois et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2004; Roseberry et al., 2004), indicating that NPY may act directly on post-synaptic targets of AgRP neurons to cause durable changes in their activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: NPY may act directly on post-synaptic targets of AgRP neurons to cause durable changes in their activity.
source: Slice recordings have shown that NPY can have persistent effects on membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release in vitro (Dubois et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2004; Roseberry et al., 2004), indicating that NPY may act directly on post-synaptic targets of AgRP neurons to cause durable changes in their activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of cited findings.

claim: Pre-stimulation of AgRP neuron axon terminals in PVH, BNST, and LH is sufficient to drive sustained feeding.
source: We have shown that pre-stimulation of AgRP neuron axon terminals in PVH, BNST, and LH is sufficient to drive sustained feeding (Chen et al., 2016), suggesting that these are the downstream sites where NPY has its long-lasting effects on hunger.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to previous work.

claim: PVH, BNST, and LH are the downstream sites where NPY has its long-lasting effects on hunger.
source: We have shown that pre-stimulation of AgRP neuron axon terminals in PVH, BNST, and LH is sufficient to drive sustained feeding (Chen et al., 2016), suggesting that these are the downstream sites where NPY has its long-lasting effects on hunger.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from cited findings.

claim: A neuropeptide that drives feeding can function on a timescale that is inaccessible to classical neurotransmitters.
source: We have shown here how a neuropeptide that drives feeding can function on a timescale that is inaccessible to classical neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: NPY allows a neuron that controls hunger to direct ongoing behavior while simultaneously anticipating and responding to impending physiologic changes.
source: This in turn allows a neuron that controls hunger to direct ongoing behavior while simultaneously anticipating and responding to impending physiologic changes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.
